readingInstruction: Read Psalm 76. It is a victory song for Zion, probably written after the Assyrian army was destroyed outside Jerusalem. Imagine the people singing it in the temple after the night the camp fell silent.
settingTheScene: Psalm 76 is a psalm of Asaph. Its mention of “Salem” and “Zion” places it in Jerusalem, and its description of warriors who “found not use of their hands” fits what happened to Sennacherib’s army in 2 Kings 19:35, when the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 men in one night. You read this psalm once in Unit 8, where the focus was on God’s presence. Here, hear it as the song after the Assyrian crisis.
observation: “In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel” (v. 1).
“His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion” (v. 2).
“There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war” (v. 3).
“The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands” (v. 5).
“At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned” (v. 6).
“But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?” (v. 7).
“From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth” (vv. 8-9).
“Make vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared” (v. 11).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a claim. In Judah God is known. This is a statement about revelation. Other nations had their gods, but the LORD made himself known in a specific people and place. His dwelling is in Zion, and from there he reveals who he is.

The picture of verse 3 is a victory without a battle on Judah’s side. The arrows, the shield, the sword are broken “there,” at Jerusalem. The enemy soldiers were stripped of their spoil and sank into sleep, the sleep of death. The mighty are helpless. The psalm does not mention Judah’s army. It was God’s victory. “At your rebuke… both rider and horse lay stunned.” In the Assyrian camp, with their chariots and horsemen, nothing was left.

The turning point is the question in verse 7: “Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?” It is not a question about the Assyrian army only. It is a question for everyone. No one can stand before God’s anger. And yet, the same verse of judgment has a purpose: “to save all the humble of the earth.” God’s judgment is a rescue for those who are oppressed. The wrath of man shall praise him, the psalm says, and the survivors of wrath will be restrained.

The psalm then calls for a response. Make vows and keep them. Bring gifts to the one to be feared. The proper response to a God who is awesome is worship and fulfilling our promises to him. And the final line is a warning to the powerful: “He cuts off the spirit of princes; he is to be feared by the kings of the earth.”

For Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem, this psalm was a testimony. The God of whom Isaiah spoke had done what he said.
connection: Jesus said that the gates of hell will not prevail against his church (Matthew 16:18). Revelation 19:11-16 shows a victorious king on a white horse. Colossians 2:15 says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them. Zephaniah 3:17 says the LORD is mighty to save. Romans 12:1 invites us to make our own offering. Hebrews 12:28-29 says our God is a consuming fire and calls for reverence.
application:
Think about a situation in which you were rescued without doing anything. Give thanks for it.

Keep a vow you have made to God and neglected.

Take comfort that God saves “all the humble of the earth.” Choose humility today.
prayerPrompts: Stand in awe of God’s name and power.
Thank him for saving the humble.
Tell him a vow you want to keep.
